run.userPrompt:
A consumer goods company sells almost entirely through third-party retailers, who control shelf placement and customer data. Management wants a direct-to-consumer channel to capture first-party data and higher margins, but its two largest retail partners together account for 55% of revenue and have punished suppliers who competed with them directly. An earlier quiet pilot of a web store triggered an angry call from one partner's buying team.

Design a go-to-market plan for building a meaningful direct-to-consumer business while keeping the retail relationships that fund the company today. Specify the channel architecture, product and pricing differentiation between channels, the data strategy, and the partner-communication plan that prevents open channel conflict.

agentRuns.userPrompt: [6,959 chars] [PREVIOUS WORK] It's worth pausing on the framing before answering it. *Defend, flank, restructure, or something else* — notice that all four are things you do to yourselves, and the disruptor appears

agentResponses.content:
Worth pausing on the framing again. "Build DTC for data and higher margins" — two goals wearing one coat, and they separate cleanly. Data requires only a *relationship* with the end customer, which no retailer can forbid. Margin requires taking *transactions*, which is precisely what they punish. Most DTC wars start because someone fused the two goals and built a transaction machine when a relationship machine would have done. The first strategic act is to split them — and to quietly retire the phrase "direct-to-consumer" in any room where a buyer might hear it. That word means "disintermediation" in their language. You are not required to speak it.

**What the angry call actually is.** Reconnaissance, bought cheap. Someone on that buying team spent political capital to tell you exactly where the tripwire sits — was it the pricing, the same SKUs, the search ads against their name? Most companies pay consultants six figures for a map of the minefield and get a worse one. Also worth mapping, just as quietly: what did the *punished* suppliers actually do? Retailers rarely punish a website. They punish being shopped against it — undercut prices, identical SKUs, leaked demand. Their fear is specific, which means it can be designed around. The silent partner, incidentally, worries me more than the one who called. The one who yells is negotiating. The quiet one may be drafting a private-label brief.

**The answer, stated once, plainly.** Build a direct *relationship* business first and a direct *transaction* business second, and make the transaction business structurally incapable of competing on the dimensions retail cares about: their price, their SKUs, their traffic. Sell what their shelves can't hold; let them sell what volume requires. Nespresso has run this architecture for decades — machines through retail at retail margins, capsules through the Club. The retailer keeps the profitable sale; the brand keeps the profitable relationship. Nobody calls anybody angry.

**Channel architecture:**

- **The flagship site as cathedral, not discounter.** Full range, storytelling, customization, exclusives, early access. Priced at MSRP, *never* discounted. It becomes the reference price — the umbrella under which retail discounting looks attractive. Your site should make their shelf price look like a deal, not the reverse.
- **Replenishment and the long tail.** Consumables, parts, accessories, subscriptions — the under-contested terrain retailers rarely fight over because shelf economics never favored it anyway. This is where DTC margin honestly lives early.
- **Certified refurbished and trade-in.** A channel partners can't easily contest, capturing the price-sensitive buyer without touching new-product price integrity. Disclose it early; it's the gray zone, and gray zones discovered are worse than gray zones announced.
- **Retail-exclusive SKUs for the top two.** Their own colors, their own bundles. This makes them co-owners of the segmentation rather than victims of it — the single cheapest peace offering available, and the one nobody thinks to give.
- **Lead routing back.** Store locator, click-and-collect, "buy" buttons that sometimes become their foot traffic. The judo move: a direct channel that *generates* demand for them is an asset they'll defend in their own meetings.

**Product and pricing differentiation, as doctrine.** Never undercut — MSRP on your site, MAP enforced everywhere. Differentiate on assortment and attachment, not price: personalization, bundles, extended warranty, service plans — value that doesn't render on a price-comparison engine. And the one unforgivable sin: the promo code. A discount email is a ratchet with a send button — it teaches your direct customers to wait, and it tells every buyer's pricing team exactly what you think their shelf is worth. Whoever runs DTC will propose one by month four. Decide now what happens then.

**Data strategy.** The product is the channel; it always was. Every unit sitting in a retail bag carries your invitation inside it — QR in the box, serial registration, an extra year of warranty for activating, an app, content worth opening. You don't need the transaction to know the customer; you need a reason. Give something for every datum, and measure the only number that matters: *what share of retail buyers become known to you within ninety days.* Then — this is the part that feels unnatural — give data back. Category insights, search trends, demand signals, quarterly, to the partners. Data given away buys the right to keep the rest. Their fear isn't that you'll learn; it's that you'll learn and they'll never see it.

**Partner communication.** No more stealth — the pilot established that discovery is worse than disclosure. Tell the top two before relaunch, individually, "you hear it from us first," and arrive with a one-page written covenant: price parity, differentiated SKUs, no undercutting, lead routing, their exclusives. Guardrails they can verify beat reassurances they must trust — and give their buying team the document they'll need to defend you internally, because that fight happens in rooms you'll never enter. Sequence the gifts before the disclosure: their exclusive SKUs and the shared data program land in the *same meeting* as the site announcement. Then keep the angry caller closest. He called because he cares; make him a design partner and he'll defend the architecture as his own idea.

**Trade-offs, honestly stated:** Parity plus exclusives means DTC economics are thin for two years — measure it as a P&L in year one and it dies, so fund it like the fire sprinkler. Differentiated SKUs cost tooling and complexity; complexity is the price of peace, but keep the count honest or it becomes the disease it cured. Registration converts a fraction, always — patience. Retail exclusives hand partners leverage; chosen once, deliberately, it's cheap. And you will never receive their customer data. Stop resenting that; build your own from the product outward.

**Sequencing.** Weeks one through six, quiet: dissect the incident, map the punished suppliers' sins, build the registration layer that needs no one's permission. Weeks six through ten: the covenant conversations, gifts in hand. Month three or four: relaunch cathedral, replenishment, refurb — with the retail exclusives shipping the same week. Twenty-four months measured on known customers, attach rates, and halo — your DTC ad spend lifting *their* sell-through, proven quarterly. Not DTC margin.

**What to watch.** Ninety-day registration rate. Replenishment attach. Partner sell-through in markets where your ads run. And the real signal, watched silently: whether private-label briefs accelerate — because the retailer was always your most dangerous competitor, and first-party data is the only defense against a gatekeeper who decides to become the brand.

The interesting question, perhaps, isn't how to go direct without angering the channel. It's why a company whose product already sits in millions of homes believes it needs permission to meet its own customers. The website is just where that meeting becomes visible. Whether the partners see a threat or a guest depends almost entirely on what you chose to put on the shelves they don't have.
